title: Support for refugee protection remains broad while confidence depends on eligibility, integration, permanence and responsibility-sharing
source_unit: Ipsos and UNHCR, Global Attitudes Towards Refugees 2026
geography: Global multi-country survey; country, generation and crisis-scenario comparisons

denominator.unit: Ipsos survey respondents across the report's participating countries; pooled respondent denominator not headlined on the public article

right_to_seek_refuge.unit: percent agreeing people should be able to take refuge in another country to escape war or persecution

claims_not_genuine.unit: percent believing many people claiming refugee status are not genuinely in need of protection

close_borders.unit: percent supporting closing borders to refugees entirely

integration_success.unit: percent believing refugees will integrate successfully into society

observations.method: Ipsos public-opinion survey conducted with UNHCR on refugee protection, claims, borders and integration.
observations.uncertainty: The pooled public article does not headline one respondent denominator; attitudes are not measures of refugee flows, asylum decisions, integration outcomes or public-service capacity.
observations.subgroup: Adults across participating countries, with country and generational comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Support for protection and suspicion about claims may reflect a desire for credible, rule-bound systems rather than opposition to refugees as a group.

observations.period: 2026; generation and country variation in integration expectations

denominator.unit: Ipsos respondents in participating countries; subgroup analytic denominators not headlined on the public article

gen_z_integration_confidence.unit: percent of Gen Z expressing confidence refugees will integrate successfully

baby_boomer_integration_confidence.unit: percent of Baby Boomers expressing confidence in successful integration

integration_generation_gap.unit: percentage-point difference between Gen Z and Baby Boomer confidence

refuge_protection_country_range.value: Support for offering refuge ranges from 78% in Sweden and the Netherlands to 44% in South Korea

observations.method: Cross-national and generational comparison of perceived integration and support for offering refuge.
observations.uncertainty: Generational differences may reflect age, cohort, political context, media exposure and national experience rather than a single age effect.
observations.subgroup: Gen Z and Baby Boomer respondents, with country comparisons across the participating markets.
observations.counterinterpretation: Younger optimism may coexist with limited practical experience of settlement systems, while older skepticism may reflect perceived pressure on existing institutions.

observations.period: 2026; public response to displacement from conflict in Iran and Lebanon

denominator.unit: Ipsos respondents considering conflict-displacement scenarios; scenario denominator not headlined on the public article

humanitarian_aid_preference.unit: percent most likely to favour humanitarian aid

diplomatic_action_preference.unit: percent most likely to favour diplomatic action

permanent_acceptance_preference.unit: percent favouring permanently accepting additional refugees

observations.method: Ipsos scenario question comparing humanitarian, diplomatic, temporary-asylum and permanent-admission responses to conflict displacement.
observations.uncertainty: Scenario preferences may not predict behavior under actual arrivals, fiscal pressure, security concerns or local service constraints; conflict framing can affect answers.
observations.subgroup: Adults in participating countries considering displacement linked to Iran and Lebanon conflicts.
observations.counterinterpretation: Preference for aid or diplomacy may express support for protection while favoring responsibility at a distance, or may reflect perceived limits of domestic reception capacity.

denominator.unit: Ipsos respondents in the comparable refugee-attitudes survey; pooled respondent denominator not headlined on the public article

ngo_responsibility.unit: percent naming NGOs as a group that should do more, up from 23%

own_government_responsibility.unit: percent naming their own government, up from 16%

wealthier_countries_responsibility.unit: percent prioritizing wealthier countries alone, down from 30%

shared_responsibility_shift.value: Responsibility is increasingly seen as distributed across international organizations, NGOs and national governments rather than assigned only to wealthy countries

observations.method: Repeated public-opinion comparison of which actors should do more to support refugees.
observations.uncertainty: Actor attribution is not willingness to pay, volunteer, host or accept policy costs; changes may reflect current conflicts and political messaging.
observations.subgroup: Adults across the participating countries in the 2025–2026 comparison.
observations.counterinterpretation: Shared responsibility language may diffuse accountability if no actor is trusted or empowered to deliver protection and integration.

related_sources.claim: Official Ipsos-UNHCR Global Attitudes Towards Refugees 2026 report PDF used for retrieval verification and hash.
Official Ipsos refugee research topic page contextualizing the 2026 survey and prior trend series.

boundary: This record adds a migration-legitimacy mechanism: support for the right to seek refuge remains broad, but public confidence is conditional on credible eligibility, integration, permanence and responsibility-sharing arrangements. It is a cross-national public-opinion survey, not an asylum adjudication dataset, refugee-integration outcome study, public-service capacity audit or forecast of migration behavior.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Ipsos article, Ipsos refugee topic page and Ipsos-UNHCR 2026 report PDF were retrieved and reviewed for refugee-protection support, claim skepticism, border closure, integration, generation and country differences, conflict scenarios and responsibility attribution; the PDF was hashed.
